title: Your career should be a series of experiments
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham opens a new WorkLife series, How to Get What You Want at Work, with author Simone Stolzoff. She observes that many people are very active in their careers without being deliberate about them, climbing the ladder until they feel bored or exhausted and then simply pushing on. Stolzoff's central insight is that you often cannot think your way into knowing what you want; you have to act your way into it. After leaving his last corporate job he treated teaching, writing a book, freelance journalism, public speaking and consulting as experiments and made decisions from the evidence. Graham connects this to her own early-career wandering across functions and notes that experiments need not mean quitting a job; a new project, responsibility or outside activity can teach what you like and what you do not. Because what you want changes over time, careers are better seen as a series of lily pads than a ladder, and the next step is to ask what small thing you could try to learn more.
points: Career treadmills keep people moving without asking what they want, so frustration arrives before deliberate reflection does.
You often cannot reason your way to the right answer; small experiments generate the data about which work is fulfilling, profitable and worth keeping.
Experiments can be low-cost, such as a new project, a different responsibility or volunteering, and learning what you dislike is equally valuable.
Preferences change across decades, so treating each decision as permanent adds needless pressure.
Replace the huge question of what to do with your life with a smaller one about what you could try that would teach you more.
quotes: many of us are incredibly active in our careers without being particularly deliberate about them.
But instead of stopping to ask ourselves what we actually want, we often just keep going. We complain about it, maybe start looking for another job, and continue pushing forward.
But one of my favorite insights from our conversation was Simone’s argument that sometimes you can’t think your way into knowing what you want. You have to act your way into it.
But how are you supposed to know whether you want to be a writer if you never write anything? How are you supposed to know whether you’d enjoy managing people if you’ve never tried leading a team?

And importantly, those experiments don’t necessarily require quitting your job or making some enormous life change. You can try a new project, take on a different responsibility, volunteer, or start doing something outside of work.
What you want at 25 probably isn’t what you’ll want at 35 or 45 or 65. Your circumstances change. Your priorities change. You change.
Simone suggests thinking of careers less like ladders and more like a series of lily pads. Sometimes you move up. Sometimes you move sideways.
What’s something I could try that would teach me more about what I want?
